mcqs.question: Why does merging two already-sorted halves of total size n cost O(n), not O(n log n)?
options: Because each element is copied out exactly once across a single forward pass over both halves
Because the merge re-sorts each half before combining them
Because only half the elements need to be compared, the rest are copied automatically
Because the log n factor comes from the merge step itself, not from repeated calls
mcqs.explanation: Every comparison in the merge advances one of the two read pointers, and every element is written to the output exactly once, so the whole merge is linear in the combined size. The log n factor comes from how many times the array gets split and merged (the recursion depth), not from any single merge call.

mcqs.question: Why is merge sort's worst case Θ(n log n), with no unlucky input the way quicksort has one?
options: Because merge sort always allocates enough auxiliary memory to avoid any slow path
Because merge sort checks if the array is already sorted before recursing
Because the recursion always splits at the exact midpoint regardless of the data, so the tree shape and per-level cost never depend on input values
Because merge sort uses randomization to avoid adversarial inputs
mcqs.explanation: The split point in merge sort is always the midpoint, independent of what the data looks like, so the recursion tree always has log n levels each costing O(n) — no input can force a deeper or costlier tree. Quicksort's split point depends on the data via the pivot, which is exactly where its O(n²) worst case comes from.

mcqs.question: In the merge step, why does breaking ties in favor of the left half (using `<=` rather than `<`) make the sort stable?
options: Because `<=` runs faster than `<` on most hardware
Because it guarantees the output array is never larger than the input
Because it avoids the need for a separate output buffer
Because elements from the left half always originated earlier in the array, so taking them first on a tie preserves their original relative order
mcqs.explanation: Stability means equal keys keep their original order. Since the left half's elements all started at earlier indices than the right half's, always resolving a tie by taking from the left preserves that ordering. Using `<` instead would let a later-positioned equal element jump ahead, breaking stability — it has nothing to do with speed or buffer size.

mcqs.question: What is the main practical difference between top-down and bottom-up merge sort?
options: Bottom-up produces a different, non-stable sort order
Top-down builds the recursion tree via recursive calls with O(log n) stack depth, while bottom-up merges increasing-size runs iteratively with no recursion
Top-down is O(n log n) while bottom-up is O(n)
Bottom-up requires the input to already be partially sorted
mcqs.explanation: Both orderings perform the identical set of merges and both are stable with the same complexity — the difference is purely structural: top-down recurses down to size 1 and merges on the way back up, while bottom-up starts by merging adjacent singletons and iteratively doubles the merge width in a loop, avoiding recursion entirely.

mcqs.question: What goes wrong if you try to merge two halves directly inside the original array, writing results into the same memory you're still reading from?
options: The output pointer can catch up to and overwrite an element the read pointers haven't consumed yet, silently corrupting the result
The recursion never terminates because the base case is never reached
It works correctly but only doubles the memory usage instead of halving it
The comparison operator must be flipped from `<=` to `<`, or the merge throws an exception
mcqs.explanation: Because the output and the two read regions occupy the same array, the write side can race ahead of a read side that hasn't finished consuming its half, overwriting data that's still needed — with no crash, just a wrong result. True in-place merging needs a genuinely different algorithm (block rotations), not just dropping the auxiliary array.
